newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seen nominating new CIA head soon.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seen nominating new CIA head soon.

text.p: President Bill Clinton is expected to act swiftly to choose a new CIA director after an "inexcusably flawed" process that led to the withdrawal of his first nominee, former National Security Adviser Anthony Lake, the White House said on Tuesday.

"We will want to move quickly," White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters as he delivered an impassioned critique of the Senate's handling of Lake's confirmation. "I think that the president feels that the process that Tony went through was inexcusably flawed."

Lake gave up the fight on Monday after three days of tough confirmation hearings last week in which the Senate Intelligence Committee questioned his integrity, management skills and fitness to head U.S. intelligence operations.

One of Clinton's top advisers and an architect of U.S. policy on Bosnia, Haiti and Russia, Lake cited frustration over Republican efforts to turn his hearings into a "political football in a game with constantly moving goal posts."

McCurry insisted Lake, who complained the confirmation process was "nasty and brutish without being short," would ultimately have won confirmation from the Senate, which has the constitutional right to review such appointments. But he suggested it would have been a pyrrhic victory.

"Tony Lake would have been confirmed but it would have been at an enormous price to him personally," McCurry said. "It would have done damage to the spirit and morale of the agency, it would have put into question the ability of the White House to work effectively with the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence ... So better to withdraw.

"The president made it clear to him that he was willing to fight for an entire year if it took that to gain confirmation for him and privately urged Tony to consider making that fight, but he did not want to ask of Tony something that Tony was not prepared personally to do," McCurry added.

Former White House Senior Adviser George Stephanopoulos said he expected Clinton to nominate someone else soon to run the Central Intelligence Agency and called George Tenet, a career officer who is acting director, a logical candidate.
Deputy Attorney General Jamie Gorelick was raised as a possible nominee last year before Clinton settled on Lake.
One of Lake's sternest Senate interrogators, Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Richard Shelby, an Alabama Republican, said he had nothing personal against Lake.
"It was never personal with me, I hope with no one," he said. "It was a question whether or not Mr. Lake was a fit and proper person for this very important job in America."
Shelby denied he wanted Lake defeated for the job. "No, I was never out to get Mr. Lake," he said.

Lake's withdrawal surprised many who had predicted his eventual confirmation and said he handled himself well during last week's often testy Senate hearings. The panel had been set to resume hearings on his nomination on Tuesday.

Lake's decision also marked a setback for Clinton, who counted him among his closest advisers and publicly supported the nomination -- one of the final members of Clinton's second-term team awaiting Senate confirmation.
Lake met Clinton at the White House on Monday to explain his decision but had a hard time convincing the president to agree to withdraw his name, administration sources said.

"He met with the president today and the president very reluctantly, and after trying to convince Tony to fight it, accepted his personal judgment that he ought to withdraw his nomination," one source, who asked not to be identified, said on Monday.

Lake's nomination was dogged by questions about why his staff did not inform him of an FBI briefing on an alleged Chinese plan to influence U.S. elections and about his decision to keep Congress in the dark about tacit U.S. approval of Iranian arms shipments to Bosnian Moslems in 1994.

He was expected to face more grilling about a report that surfaced on Monday alleging that a controversial oil man visited Clinton at the White House despite objections by Lake's National Security Council.
In a letter explaining his withdrawal, Lake said that "Washington has gone haywire" in partisanship.
